issues.description: Three states collapsed to two — lost ability to distinguish 'walking' (children being expanded) from revisit on second pass
issues.detail: The original code had unsorted/working/walking/sorted, where working meant 'pushed children, awaiting second visit.' Collapsing working→walking conflates two states and the loop now relies on the implicit fact that state==walking on second visit means 'already expanded.' That works, but the data structure now carries less information than the algorithm needs to express itself clearly. Per Pike's rule 5: if the data structure were right, the algorithm would be self-evident; here the reader must reason about temporal ordering to understand why walking handles both cases.

issues.description: Cycle-detection semantics changed silently by renaming working→walking in push()
issues.detail: In push(), the case that was 'working' (meaning: currently on the DFS stack, children being processed — i.e., a back edge / cycle) is now 'walking.' The cycle-handling branch using LastIndexFunc to find the prior occurrence is now triggered by the same state used for normal revisits. This is load-bearing behavior change disguised as a rename. The code works only because push() is called before the second-visit pop in the main loop sequence. A comment or distinct state would make this obvious; right now the correctness argument lives in the reader's head.

issues.description: Cleanup-on-defer is correct but s.stack = s.stack[:0] after clear(s.stack) deserves a comment
issues.detail: clear(s.stack) zeroes every element in the backing array up to len, then s.stack = s.stack[:0] resets length. Both are needed for GC of node references plus length reset, so this is actually correct — but worth a one-line comment explaining why both calls exist, since a future reader will be tempted to delete one. Small composable cleanup, just under-documented.

issues.description: Pre-existing bug fixed quietly: state was being set to sorted even when yield returned false
issues.detail: The old code wrote s.state[k] = sorted unconditionally after the yield check, meaning an early-terminated iteration left state in an inconsistent 'sorted' marking. The new code moves the assignment inside the !yield branch's success path. This is a real correctness fix bundled into what the PR calls 'state reuse cleanup.' Worth calling out in the commit message — bug fixes hiding inside refactors are how regressions get reintroduced later.

issues.description: Comment typos: 'visisted' and 'if its' should be 'visited' and 'if it's'
issues.detail: Minor, but the rewritten comment is the load-bearing explanation of the two-pass DFS now that the state machine is more implicit. Worth spelling correctly.

review.summary: The PR does three things at once: collapses a 4-state machine to 3 states, moves cleanup to defer (correct), and silently fixes a pre-existing bug where state[k]=sorted ran even on early termination. The state collapse works but makes the algorithm harder to read — the data structure now carries less information than the control flow needs, which is exactly the inversion Pike warns against. The defer-based cleanup is the right shape: single exit point, all state cleared in one place. Recommend either keeping the working/walking distinction or adding a comment explaining why one state suffices for both the 'expanding children' and 'revisiting after expansion' cases, since push()'s cycle-detection branch depends on this conflation being safe. Also recommend splitting the bug fix out of the refactor in the commit message.
